flashcards.q: What two structural properties make CNNs beat MLPs on images, and give the parameter-count comparison.
flashcards.a: Weight sharing (one kernel reused at every spatial position) and translation equivariance (shift input -> shift output correspondingly). A 3x3x64x64 conv kernel has 36,864 params regardless of image size; an equivalent MLP layer on a 224x224x64 feature map would need on the order of 10^13 weights.

flashcards.q: State the convolution output-size formula and compute it for in=224, kernel=7, stride=2, padding=3.
flashcards.a: out = floor((in + 2*pad - kernel)/stride) + 1. floor((224+6-7)/2)+1 = floor(223/2)+1 = 111+1 = 112. This is exactly ResNet's stem layer, halving 224 to 112.

flashcards.q: What is the degradation problem ResNet solved, and how is it different from vanishing gradients?
flashcards.a: Past a certain depth, plain stacked CNNs got WORSE training error, not just validation error -- an optimization failure, not overfitting. It's distinct from sigmoid-style vanishing gradients because ResNet used ReLU (no saturation on the positive side); the actual issue was that stacked nonlinear layers struggled to learn an identity mapping, which skip connections (y=F(x)+x) sidestep directly.

flashcards.q: By what factor did AlexNet reduce ImageNet top-5 error versus the prior best approach, and what three techniques made it feasible?
flashcards.a: From ~26% (SIFT+SVM era) to 15.3% in 2012, roughly a 40% relative reduction. Made feasible by ReLU (no saturating-activation ceiling), dropout (controls overfitting on ~60M params), and GPU training (feasible wall-clock time).

flashcards.q: At what data scale does ViT start to beat CNNs, per the original ViT paper's own results?
flashcards.a: ViT underperforms ResNets when trained from scratch on ImageNet-1k alone (~1.3M images); results are mixed at ImageNet-21k (~14M); ViT clearly overtakes CNN baselines at JFT-300M scale (~300M images). Practical rule of thumb: below ~100M pretraining images, bet on a CNN or a pretrained ViT, not a from-scratch ViT.

flashcards.q: Describe ViT's patch embedding pipeline for a 224x224 image with 16x16 patches, including the token count.
flashcards.a: Split into (224/16)^2 = 196 non-overlapping 16x16 patches, flatten and linearly project each to the embedding dim, prepend a learnable [CLS] token, add positional embeddings (attention has no inherent spatial order), feed the resulting 197-token sequence to a standard transformer encoder.

flashcards.q: Trace the detection lineage R-CNN to Faster R-CNN to YOLO to DETR, naming the specific pain each step fixed.
flashcards.a: R-CNN (2014): ~2000 separately-cropped region proposals per image, extremely slow. Faster R-CNN (2015): learned Region Proposal Network sharing backbone features, much faster but still two-stage. YOLO (2016): single forward pass regresses boxes+classes directly, real-time but historically weaker on small/overlapping objects. DETR (2020): set prediction via object queries + bipartite matching, eliminates anchors and NMS, but has slow convergence and weak small-object performance from global attention.

flashcards.q: What is SAM (Segment Anything Model) and how is its architecture split for interactive use?
flashcards.a: A promptable segmentation model (Kirillov et al. 2023) trained on SA-1B (11M images, 1.1B masks) that produces a valid mask given a point/box/mask prompt with no task-specific fine-tuning. Architecture splits work for speed: a heavier ViT-based image encoder runs once per image; a lightweight prompt encoder + mask decoder run per-prompt in milliseconds, enabling near-instant interactive re-prompting.

flashcards.q: What does batch norm normalize, and why does it sometimes hurt during fine-tuning with small batches?
flashcards.a: It normalizes each channel's activations to zero mean/unit variance across the mini-batch (train time), then applies a learned scale/shift; at eval time it uses running statistics. With small batch sizes, the per-batch mean/variance estimates are noisy and running stats may not stabilize, causing a train/eval mismatch -- fix with GroupNorm/LayerNorm instead.

flashcards.q: Why does stacking two 3x3 convolutions give the same receptive field as one 5x5 convolution with fewer parameters?
flashcards.a: Two stacked 3x3 convs reach a 5x5 effective receptive field using 2x9=18 weight positions, versus 25 for a single 5x5 conv -- fewer parameters for the same receptive field, plus an extra nonlinearity between them. This was VGG's argument for using stacks of small kernels.

flashcards.q: What is the standard transfer-learning default for a new vision task, and when do you freeze the backbone vs fully fine-tune it?
flashcards.a: Take a backbone pretrained on ImageNet (or larger), replace the head. Freeze the backbone and train only the head when data is limited and the target domain is visually similar to natural photos. Fully fine-tune at a low LR (~1e-4 to 1e-5, often with discriminative per-layer LRs) when you have more data and/or the target domain (satellite, medical) is visually distant from natural photos.

flashcards.q: What does U-Net add to a plain encoder-decoder segmentation architecture, and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: Skip connections between corresponding encoder and decoder resolutions, so fine spatial detail lost during downsampling is recovered during upsampling. Without them, segmentation masks come out blocky/low-resolution around object boundaries.

flashcards.q: What NMS-free innovation did Ultralytics YOLO26 (Jan 2026) introduce, and what earlier architecture pioneered the underlying idea?
flashcards.a: YOLO26 does native end-to-end NMS-free inference (removing Distribution Focal Loss, adding Progressive Loss Balancing and Small-Target-Aware Label Assignment). The underlying idea of eliminating post-hoc box suppression traces back to DETR's set-prediction framing from 2020.
